title: Everyday colloquial Turkish
seoTitle: Colloquial Turkish: abi, abla, şey, yani
intro: This unit is about everyday, spoken Turkish: how to address people (*abi*, *hocam*, *beyefendi*), how to soften a request (*Bir bakar mısın?*, *Gelsene*), the words that fill a pause (*şey*, *yani*, *falan*), the suffixes that make a word small, dear, pitiful or approximate (*küçücük*, *adamcağız*, *yeşilimsi*), and how one request moves from formal to colloquial.

blocks.text: English often addresses a stranger with nothing at all: **Excuse me, is this the bus to the centre?** Turkish likes to name the person, and the word it picks says how old they are compared with you, what they do and how formal the moment is. Many of these words come from the family: you call a shopkeeper a little older than you *abi* (big brother) and a woman your grandmother's age *teyze* (auntie), without being related at all.

head: Word
Say it to
Example
rows: a man a little older than you; friendly
*Abi, bu otobüs Kadıköy'e gidiyor mu?* (Excuse me, does this bus go to Kadıköy?)
a woman a little older than you; friendly
*Abla, simit kaç lira?* (How much is a simit?)
a younger person, usually a young man
*Kardeşim, bir yardım eder misin?* (Mate, could you give me a hand?)
an older woman, about your mother's or grandmother's age
*Amca, çantanızı taşıyayım mı?* (Shall I carry your bag?)
a teacher or lecturer; in many offices, a colleague
*Hocam, bir sorum var.* (Excuse me, I have a question.)
a craftsman, a mechanic, a cook, a driver
*Usta, müsait bir yerde inebilir miyim?* (Could you let me off somewhere convenient?)
a man you don't know, politely
*Beyefendi, cüzdanınız düştü.* (Sir, you've dropped your wallet.)
a woman you don't know, politely

blocks.text: **Sen or siz?** The family words are warm and usually go with *sen*: *Abi, bakar mısın?* With an older stranger many people still use *siz* (*Teyze, buyurun, oturun*), and *beyefendi* and *hanımefendi* always take *siz*: *Beyefendi, buyurun* sounds right, *Beyefendi, gel buraya* sounds rude.

**With a name.** For someone you know, put *abi*, *abla*, *teyze* or *amca* after the first name: *Ali abi*, *Fatma teyze*. In writing these keep a small letter, because they are family words; the titles *Bey* and *Hanım* of [A1 unit 3](a1-u03) take a capital: *Murat Bey*, *Ayşe Hanım*. *Bey* and *Hanım* are the polite choice with colleagues, neighbours and customers; *Bay* and *Bayan* belong on forms and doors, not in speech.

**Hocam** is *hoca* (teacher) with the possessive **my**. Students say it to teachers at every level, and in universities and many offices it has become a friendly, respectful way to address a colleague. **Usta** (master) does the same for anyone who works with their hands: the mechanic, the cook at the kebab shop, the driver of a *dolmuş*.

**Terms of endearment.** Family and friends use the possessive too: *canım* (my dear, from *can*, life), *kızım* (my girl), *oğlum* (my boy), *evladım* (my child). Older people say them to any young person, warmly. A diminutive makes them tenderer still: *anneciğim*, *babacığım* ([see below](gp-diminutives)).

items.en: Excuse me (to a teacher), I have a question.

items.tr: Usta, müsait bir yerde inebilir miyim?
items.en: Could you let me off somewhere convenient? (to a driver)

items.tr: Pardon beyefendi, bu yer boş mu?
items.en: Excuse me, sir, is this seat free?
Darling, what shall we eat tonight?
Mate, where's the bus stop?

blocks.text: *Abi* and *abla* are friendly, not rude, but they assume a relaxed setting: in a bank or a hotel, say *beyefendi*, *hanımefendi* or nothing. *Kardeşim* said sharply can sound like **listen, pal**: *Kardeşim, sıraya gir!* (Get in the queue, pal!)

sections.title: Bir bakar mısın? Softening a request

blocks.text: A bare imperative (*Kapıyı kapat*) is fine with family, but most requests are softened, and people combine several tools at once.

head: Tool
Example
Meaning and feel
rows: Could you close the door? Everyday, neutral.
Could you just take a look? Lighter: just, for a moment.
Could you close the door? Polite.
Close the door, will you? Friendly, insistent.
If it's no trouble, could you close the door? Very polite.
Could I have a glass of water? Polite, a little formal.
If you're free, could we talk a little? Polite.

blocks.text: **Bir** here isn't **one**. Unstressed and right before the verb, it means **just, for a moment**, and makes the request smaller: *Bir bakar mısınız?* is the standard way to call a waiter or a shop assistant (you met *Bakar mısınız?* in [A2 unit 4](gp-aorist-uses)); *Bir dakika gelir misin?* (Could you come here a minute?). In quick speech it often sounds like *bi*.

**-sAnA.** Added to the verb stem, `-sAnA` (`-sAnIzA` for *siz*) makes a friendly push, half suggestion, half order: *Gelsene!* (Come on, come over!), *Otursana* (Sit down, why don't you), *Baksana!* (Hey, look!). The voice decides whether it is warm or impatient: *Dinlesene!* can be **Listen to this!** or **Will you listen!** The negative, `-mAsAnA`, tells someone to stop: *Bağırmasana!* (Stop shouting, will you!). There is no question form.

rows.en: stop shouting, will you (to one person)
stop shouting, will you (to several people)

blocks.text: **Conditionals that ask.** A conditional without its main clause sounds tentative, like **what if I…?**: *Pencereyi açsam?* (What if I opened the window?), *Bir çay daha içsek?* (How about another tea?), from [B1 unit 9](gp-sa-advice). *Rica etsem* (literally **if I requested**) turns this into a polite request: *Bir bardak su rica etsem?* (Could I have a glass of water?), *Sizden bir şey rica etsem?* (Could I ask you a favour?).

**Zahmet olmazsa** (if it's no trouble) and **mümkünse** (if possible) go in front of a polite question: *Zahmet olmazsa tuzu uzatır mısınız?* (Would you mind passing the salt?). Before asking, people often apologize for the bother: *Affedersiniz…* (Excuse me…), *Kusura bakmayın, rahatsız ediyorum ama…* (Sorry to bother you, but…). The usual answers are *Tabii*, *Olur* and, to thanks for the trouble, *Ne zahmeti!* (No trouble at all!).

items.en: Excuse me! (to a waiter)
Come on, the film's starting!
Would you mind passing the salt?
Stop shouting, the baby's asleep!
Could I ask you something?

blocks.text: `-sAnA` is for people you say *sen* to, or a group of friends (`-sAnIzA`). With a stranger or a superior it is too pushy: to a teacher, say *Hocam, bir bakar mısınız?*, not *Hocam, baksanıza*.

sections.title: Şey, yani, falan: filling the gaps

blocks.text: Conversation needs words that buy time, soften a point or round off a list. A learner who never uses them sounds like a book; one who uses nothing else sounds like a teenager. These seven are the core.

head: Word
As a filler
Example
rows: um, er; thingy (a word you can't find)
*Şey… adı neydi, o dizi?* (Um… what was it called, that series?)
you know; well, there you go
*İşte, öyle bir şey.* (Well, it's something like that.)
*Hani şu yeni dizi var ya?* (You know that new series?)
*Aslında ben pek sevmedim.* (Actually, I didn't like it much.)
*Yarım saat falan bekledik.* (We waited half an hour or so.)

blocks.text: **Şey** (thing) stands in for a word you can't find, and on its own it fills a pause: *Şey… nasıl desem…* (Um… how can I put it…). It even takes the case ending of the noun it replaces: *Şeyi gördün mü, kumandayı?* (Have you seen the thingy, the remote?).
**Yani** (that is) explains, sums up or draws a conclusion: *Film uzundu, yani üç saat!* (The film was long, I mean three hours!). On its own, as a question, *Yani?* means **So?** or **So what?**

**İşte** and **hani** you met as particles in [B2 unit 8](gp-modal-particles). As fillers they keep a story moving: *Dün işte arkadaşlarla çıktık, işte bir kafeye gittik…* (Yesterday, you know, we went out with friends, went to a café…). *Hani* points to something the listener should remember: *Hani dün bahsettiğim film…* (You know, the film I mentioned yesterday…).

**Ya** at the end of a sentence adds feeling, and is often stretched in speech: *Çok güzel ya!* (It's so lovely!), *Of ya, yine geç kaldık!* (Ugh, we're late again!). At the start, it brushes something aside: *Ya, bırak şimdi!* (Oh, forget it!). This is not the reminding *ya* of [B2 unit 8](gp-ya-particle), which follows something the listener already knows.

**Falan** (also *filan*) ends a list or makes a number approximate: *Çay, kahve falan içtik* (We had tea, coffee and so on), *Yirmi kişi falan vardı* (There were twenty people or so). *Falan filan* is **and so on and so forth**.

**A few more.** *Peki* (OK, well then) accepts or moves on; *neyse* (anyway) closes a topic; *aynen* (exactly) agrees; *cidden* (seriously) asks for or gives emphasis: *Cidden mi?* (Seriously?); *mesela* (for example) brings in an example.

items.en: Um… I had a question.

items.tr: Yani bu akşam gelmiyorsun, öyle mi?
items.en: So you're not coming tonight, is that it?

items.tr: Hani şu yeni dizi var ya, çok güzelmiş.
items.en: You know that new series? Apparently it's really good.

items.tr: Aslında ben o filmi pek sevmedim.
items.en: Actually, I didn't really like that film.
Anyway, we'll talk tomorrow.

blocks.text: In writing and in formal speech, leave the fillers out. And don't stack them: *Yani şey işte falan…* tells your listener you have nothing to say.

sections.title: Küçücük, adamcağız, yeşilimsi: small, dear, pitiful, -ish

blocks.text: Four suffixes shade a word rather than change it: `-CIk` makes it small or dear, `-CAğIz` pitiful, and `-(I)msI` and `-(I)mtırak` only roughly so, like English **-ish**. All four belong to everyday, emotional speech.

**-CIk on adjectives** makes a small thing smaller or a pleasant quality cosier: *küçücük* (tiny), *sıcacık bir çorba* (a lovely warm soup). The common forms are best learned as words: a final k drops (*küçük* → *küçücük*), and a one-syllable adjective often adds a vowel (*az* → *azıcık*). The C becomes ç after a voiceless consonant, as in `-CI` ([A2 unit 12](gp-ci)), but most of these words end in a vowel or a voiced consonant.

**-CIk with words for people.** On *anne*, *baba* and other words you call people by, `-CIk` with the possessive is pure affection: *anneciğim* (mum dear), *babacığım*, *teyzeciğim*, *ablacığım*. The k softens to ğ before the vowel of the possessive: *anne-cik* → *anne-ciğ-im*.

**-CAğIz** (pitiful). After a noun for a person, it shows sympathy: *adamcağız* (the poor man), *kadıncağız* (the poor woman), *kızcağız* (the poor girl), *çocukcağız* (the poor child), *hayvancağız* (the poor animal). It belongs to storytelling, usually in the third person: *Adamcağız saatlerce bekledi* (The poor man waited for hours). The adjective *zavallı* (poor, pitiful) does the same job in front of the noun, and the two often go together: *zavallı adamcağız*.

**-(I)msI and -(I)mtırak** (-ish) work on colours, tastes and a few other adjectives: *yeşilimsi* (greenish), *mavimsi* (bluish), *ekşimsi* (sourish), *tatlımsı* (sweetish). `-(I)msI` follows four-way harmony and adds its first vowel only after a consonant: *mavi-msi*, *sarı-msı*, *yeşil-imsi*, *mor-umsu*. `-(I)mtırak` means the same, works on fewer words, and keeps its own vowels after the first: *ekşimtırak*, *yeşilimtırak*, *sarımtırak*.

items.en: They live in a tiny flat.
Mum dear, I'm really tired today.
The poor man waited hours for the bus.
The sea was a greenish colour.
These apples are a bit sourish.
Would you like a drop more tea?

blocks.text: `-CIk` and `-CAğIz` are colloquial and emotional: right in a story or a chat, out of place in a report. And not every word takes them; if you haven't heard a form, say *çok küçük*, *biraz yeşil* or *zavallı adam* instead.
*Yeşilimsi* and *yeşilimtırak* are French **verdâtre**; *sıcacık* and *küçücük* are close to **tout chaud** and **tout petit**.

The same request comes out very differently in an official notice, with a colleague and among friends. Choosing a register means choosing several things together: *siz* or *sen*, the verb form, the way you address the person, and the small words.

blocks.caption: The same requests in three registers
head: Request
Formal
Neutral
Colloquial

blocks.text: **Formal** Turkish, in letters, notices and announcements ([B2 unit 5](gp-formal-requests)), uses *siz*, the long imperative `-(y)InIz`, *rica ederim* after a `-mA` clause ([B2 unit 4](gp-reported-commands)), and words like *yardımcı olmak* (to be of help) or *bilgi vermek* (to inform). **Neutral** Turkish, the safe choice with anyone you don't know well, asks a question with *siz*: `-(y)AbilIr misiniz?` or the aorist, with *lütfen* or *bir*. **Colloquial** Turkish, with friends and family, uses *sen*, `-sAnA`, *bir*, the fillers, and an address word: *abi*, *canım*.

items.tr: Sayın izleyicilerimiz, yayınımıza kısa bir ara veriyoruz.
items.en: Dear viewers, we are taking a short break. (formal: a TV announcer)
Could you turn the TV down a little? (neutral)
Turn that TV down a bit, will you! (colloquial)
Shall we push the meeting to tomorrow? (colloquial)

blocks.text: When in doubt, choose neutral: *siz* and a question with `-(y)AbilIr misiniz?` never offends. Moving to *sen* is usually the older or more senior person's offer: *Bana sen diyebilirsin* (You can say *sen* to me).
Formal letters, requests with `-mAsInI rica etmek`, and suggestions with `-sA`.

summary: Strangers are addressed by age and role: *abi*, *abla*, *kardeşim*, *teyze*, *amca* (friendly, mostly with *sen*), *hocam*, *usta*, and politely *beyefendi* and *hanımefendi* (always with *siz*). After a name: *Ali abi* (small letter), *Ayşe Hanım* (capital).

Soften a request with an aorist question and *bir* (*Bir bakar mısınız?*), with `-(y)AbilIr misiniz?`, *zahmet olmazsa* or *rica etsem*. `-sAnA` (*Gelsene!*) is a friendly push for *sen*; `-mAsAnA` (*Bağırmasana!*) asks someone to stop.
Fillers: *şey* (um; thingy), *yani* (I mean, so), *işte* and *hani* (you know), *ya* (feeling), *aslında* (actually), *falan* (and stuff, or so); also *peki*, *neyse*, *aynen*, *cidden*, *mesela*.
`-CIk` makes small or cosy (*küçücük*, *sıcacık*, *azıcık*) and dear (*anneciğim*); `-CAğIz` pitiful (*adamcağız*); `-(I)msI` and `-(I)mtırak` mean **-ish** (*yeşilimsi*, *ekşimtırak*).
Formal, neutral and colloquial requests differ in person (*siz*, *sen*), verb form (`-mAnızı rica ederim`, `-(y)AbilIr misiniz?`, `-sAnA`), address and particles. Neutral is the safe default.
